questions.title: What are Core Web Vitals and why do they matter?
questions.quick: Core Web Vitals are a small set of user-centric metrics, defined by Google, that quantify real-world page experience. There are three: Largest Contentful Paint for loading, Interaction to Next Paint for responsiveness, and Cumulative Layout Shift for visual stability. I would explain them as: did the main content show up quickly, does the page react when I tap, and does it stay still while I read. They matter for users, conversion, and as a search ranking signal, though content relevance still outweighs them.
questions.revision: Core Web Vitals = LCP (loading), INP (responsiveness), CLS (visual stability): three field-measured user-experience metrics, judged on real-user data.
questions.detailed:
**Core Web Vitals (CWV)** are the subset of web performance metrics that Google considers essential to a good user experience. Each one maps to a question a real visitor implicitly asks:

| Metric | Question it answers | Aspect |
|---|---|---|
| **LCP** (Largest Contentful Paint) | Did the main content appear quickly? | Loading |
| **INP** (Interaction to Next Paint) | Does the page respond promptly when I interact? | Responsiveness |
| **CLS** (Cumulative Layout Shift) | Does content jump around while I use it? | Visual stability |

## How they work
- They are measured in the browser, on real visitors' devices, and aggregated as **field data** (for example through the Chrome UX Report). Lab tools can estimate them but are not the source of truth.
- Each metric has a "good / needs improvement / poor" band, and a page or origin passes when the **75th percentile** of visits is in the good band (see the thresholds question).
- The set is not frozen: Google has revised it over time. INP replaced First Input Delay (FID) as the responsiveness metric in March 2024.

## Why they matter
- **Users and business**: slow, janky or shifting pages lose engagement and conversions, especially on mid-range phones and weak networks.
- **Search**: they feed Google's page experience signals. They are one ranking input among many, so do not oversell them as a trump card over relevant content.
- **Engineering**: they give teams a shared, measurable vocabulary and a target for budgets and regression alerts.

## Common mistakes
- Treating a single Lighthouse score as "our Core Web Vitals".
- Optimising only the homepage while templates such as product, listing and checkout pages are measured separately.
- Forgetting that other metrics (TTFB, FCP, TBT) are diagnostic aids, not Core Web Vitals themselves.

questions.title: What are the Core Web Vitals thresholds, and what does the 75th percentile mean?
questions.quick: The good thresholds are LCP at or under 2.5 seconds, INP at or under 200 milliseconds, and CLS at or under 0.1. A page passes a metric when the 75th percentile of real visits meets the good threshold, meaning at least three quarters of page loads are good. Poor starts above 4 seconds for LCP, 500 milliseconds for INP, and 0.25 for CLS. Using the 75th percentile stops averages from hiding a slow tail and stops rare outliers from dominating.
questions.revision: Good: LCP ≤2.5s, INP ≤200ms, CLS ≤0.1, each judged at the 75th percentile of real page loads, segmented by mobile and desktop.
questions.detailed:
**Thresholds to memorise**

| Metric | Good | Needs improvement | Poor |
|---|---|---|---|
| LCP | ≤ 2.5 s | 2.5 to 4 s | > 4 s |
| INP | ≤ 200 ms | 200 to 500 ms | > 500 ms |
| CLS | ≤ 0.1 | 0.1 to 0.25 | > 0.25 |

## What "75th percentile" means
Take all real page loads of a URL (or origin) over a period, sort each metric's values, and read the value at the 75th percentile. If that value is in the good band, the page **passes** that metric. In plain terms: at least 75% of visits had a good experience.

The assessment is made **per metric and per device class** (mobile and desktop reported separately). A page passes Core Web Vitals overall only if all three metrics pass.

## Why the 75th percentile and not the average or median
- The **average** is distorted by a few extreme values and hides how bad the slow tail is.
- The **median** (p50) would let a quarter of users have a poor experience yet still pass.
- A higher percentile such as p95 would be dominated by outliers (very old devices, flaky networks) that the team cannot reasonably fix.
- p75 is a pragmatic compromise: it forces the team to care about the slower quarter of users while staying stable.

## Practical consequences
- A lab run that reports 2.1 s LCP does not mean you pass; your real p75 could still be 3.4 s because users have slower devices and networks.
- Field data in the Chrome UX Report is a rolling window (commonly 28 days), so improvements take weeks to be fully visible. Use your own RUM for faster feedback.
- Improvement means moving the slow tail, so test on throttled mid-range hardware, not a developer laptop.

## Common mistake
Quoting the three numbers without saying they are percentile-based and field-measured. That is the detail interviewers listen for.

questions.title: What is Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) and which element counts?
questions.quick: LCP is the time from the start of navigation until the largest visible content element in the viewport has finished rendering. It is a proxy for when the main content feels loaded. The candidate is usually a hero image, a large heading or text block, or a poster image on a video. On a vehicle detail page it would likely be the main vehicle photo. The target is 2.5 seconds or less at the 75th percentile, and the element can change as the page loads.
questions.revision: LCP = render time of the largest image or text block in the viewport. Good is 2.5s or less at p75; the first step is always identifying the element.
questions.detailed: **LCP measures when the largest content element visible in the viewport is rendered.** It approximates "when did the user see the main thing they came for?". ## Which elements are candidates - `` elements (including those inside ``) - `` inside SVG, and `

questions.title: What causes poor LCP, and what are its four sub-parts?
questions.quick: I break LCP into four sub-parts: time to first byte, resource load delay, resource load duration, and element render delay. Poor LCP usually comes from a slow server or missing edge caching, the LCP resource being discovered late, an oversized image, render-blocking CSS or JavaScript, or client-side rendering that only creates the element after a large bundle runs. Slow web fonts can delay text LCP. Splitting the time this way tells me which layer to fix.
questions.revision: LCP time = TTFB + resource load delay + resource load duration + element render delay. Find the largest slice before optimising anything.
questions.detailed:
A poor LCP is a symptom. The useful move is to decompose the time into the four sub-parts defined in Google's guidance and find which dominates.

{{diagram:lcp-parts}}

| Sub-part | What it is | Typical culprits |
|---|---|---|
| **TTFB** | Navigation start to first HTML byte | Slow origin or SSR, no CDN caching, redirects, cold starts |
| **Resource load delay** | TTFB to when the browser *starts* fetching the LCP resource | Hero injected by JavaScript, CSS background image, lazy-loaded hero, low priority |
| **Resource load duration** | Time to download the resource | Oversized or poorly compressed image, distant origin, bandwidth contention |
| **Element render delay** | Resource ready to element painted | Render-blocking CSS/JS, long main-thread tasks, hydration, web font blocking |

Google's guidance suggests that in a well-tuned page most of the time is split between TTFB and load duration, while load delay and render delay should be small. Treat those proportions as a heuristic, not a rule.

## Other recurring causes
- Too much JavaScript to download, parse and execute before content is usable.
- Late-loaded hero content that depends on an API call after hydration.
- Slow fonts when the LCP is a heading.
- Third-party scripts competing for bandwidth and CPU.

## Example reasoning
If TTFB is 1.8 s and the image downloads in 0.4 s, compressing the image will barely help; the fix is caching and server response. If TTFB is 0.3 s but the image request starts at 2.2 s, the problem is discovery, so fix the markup or priority.

## Common mistake
Jumping to "compress the image" for every LCP problem without measuring which sub-part is large.

questions.title: How do you improve LCP?
questions.quick: I attack the largest sub-part first. Reduce TTFB with CDN edge caching, an efficient backend and fast SSR. Make the LCP image discoverable in the initial HTML, never lazy-loaded, and give it high fetch priority. Serve right-sized responsive images in AVIF or WebP through a CDN. Remove render-blocking CSS and JavaScript from the critical path, and cut JavaScript through code splitting and tree shaking. Then validate in both lab and real-user data.
questions.revision: Improve LCP in order: faster first byte, discover the hero early, shrink and prioritise the image, unblock rendering, trim JavaScript.
questions.detailed: LCP is improved by shortening whichever sub-part dominates. A practical checklist, in priority order: ## 1. Cut TTFB - Serve HTML from a CDN where possible; cache or use stale-while-revalidate for pages that are not personalised. - Avoid redirect chains and slow origin work (database calls, uncached API calls during SSR). - Stream HTML so the browser gets the head and first content early. ## 2. Make the LCP resource discoverable and prioritised - Put the hero in the server HTML as a real ``, not injected by client JavaScript and not a CSS background. - **Never lazy-load the LCP image.** Use `fetchpriority="high"` on it. - Preload only when the browser cannot find it in markup early. ```html ``` ## 3. Optimise the bytes - Modern formats (AVIF or WebP with a fallback where needed), correct dimensions, sensible compression and `srcset`/`sizes`. - Deliver through a CDN with long-lived cache headers. ## 4. Unblock rendering - Inline or split critical CSS, defer non-critical CSS, add `defer`/`async` to scripts, and avoid blocking font loads. ## 5. Reduce JavaScript - Code splitting, tree shaking, removing unused dependencies, deferring third parties. Less JS means less contention and a shorter render delay. ## Common mistakes - Preloading many resources, which dilutes priority. - Using JavaScript-driven image components that delay discovery. - Declaring victory from one Lighthouse run instead of checking field data.

questions.title: What is INP, and why did it replace FID?
questions.quick: INP, Interaction to Next Paint, measures how quickly the page visually responds after a user clicks, taps or presses a key, across the whole visit. It reports roughly the slowest interaction, and good is 200 milliseconds or less. It replaced First Input Delay in March 2024 because FID only measured the delay before the very first interaction started processing. INP covers all interactions and includes event handler time and the time to paint the result.
questions.revision: INP = latency of interactions across the visit, input delay + processing + presentation, roughly the worst one; good ≤200ms. It replaced FID in March 2024.
questions.detailed:
**INP (Interaction to Next Paint)** observes the latency of every click, tap and key press during a page visit and reports a value representative of the worst of them (for pages with very many interactions, a high percentile-like pick that ignores outliers). Scrolling and hovering are not counted.

## What one interaction contains
{{diagram:inp-phases}}

1. **Input delay**: waiting because the main thread is busy.
2. **Processing time**: running event handlers (and any React updates they trigger).
3. **Presentation delay**: recalculating style/layout and painting the next frame.

The clock stops at the **next paint** after the interaction, so visual feedback is what matters, not merely that code ran.

## Example
A shopper taps "Configure vehicle". If a 500 ms JavaScript task runs before the UI changes, INP for that interaction is about 500 ms: poor, because above 500 ms is "poor" and 200 ms or less is "good".

## Why INP replaced FID
| | FID | INP |
|---|---|---|
| Which interactions | First only | All during the visit |
| What is timed | Input delay only | Delay + handlers + rendering |
| Typical result | Almost always passed | Exposes real sluggishness |

FID could pass while the page felt janky after load because it ignored later interactions and the cost of handling them. INP is a far better proxy for perceived responsiveness.

## Common mistakes
- Saying "FID" in a current interview without noting it was retired as a Core Web Vital.
- Thinking INP is only about the handler: input delay and rendering also count.
- Testing only the first click after page load.

questions.title: What causes poor INP?
questions.quick: Poor INP almost always means the main thread is busy when the user interacts or when the result must be painted. Typical causes are long JavaScript tasks, heavy event handlers, excessive React re-renders from badly placed state or context, large component trees and big lists, expensive synchronous calculations, large DOM updates that make layout and paint slow, and third-party scripts such as tag managers and widgets competing for the same thread.
questions.revision: Poor INP = busy main thread: long tasks, heavy handlers, over-rendering, large DOM, third-party scripts delaying input, handlers, or the next paint.
questions.detailed:
INP is bad when the main thread cannot get to the interaction promptly, cannot finish the handler quickly, or cannot paint the result quickly. Map causes to the three phases.

## Input delay (main thread busy before the handler runs)
- Long tasks (over 50 ms) from hydration, bundle evaluation, or timers.
- Third-party scripts (tag managers, chat widgets, ad code) running during or after load.

## Processing time (handlers are slow)
- Heavy synchronous work inside click handlers: filtering big arrays, JSON parsing, price calculations.
- Excessive React rendering: state held too high in the tree, a context whose value changes on every update, unmemoised large lists, no virtualisation.
- Analytics or logging done synchronously inside the handler.

## Presentation delay (the next frame is expensive)
- A very large DOM, or updates that touch thousands of nodes.
- Forced synchronous layout (reading layout properties after writes in loops).
- Expensive CSS selectors, big style recalculations, heavy paint effects.

## Example
A configurator page re-renders every option card when any option changes because selection state lives in a top-level context. Each click takes 400 ms, so INP is poor although the network is fast.

## Why the cause differs from LCP's
LCP usually reflects network and resource discovery. INP is almost entirely CPU-bound on the main thread, so **slower phones suffer disproportionately**; a fast laptop hides the problem.

## Common mistakes
- Fixing only your own code when a third-party script holds the thread.
- Assuming virtual DOM makes rendering free.
- Measuring only the first interaction, after load, when hydration has finished.

questions.title: How do you improve INP?
questions.quick: I first find which interactions are slow, then shrink main-thread work. Ship less JavaScript through code splitting. Break long tasks into smaller chunks and yield to the browser between them. In React, fix state placement, context churn and large lists, and use memoisation only where profiling shows a win. Mark non-urgent updates with transitions. Show immediate visual feedback, and defer analytics and other non-critical work so it never blocks the next paint.
questions.revision: Improve INP by finding slow interactions, cutting JS, splitting long tasks, yielding, trimming React renders, giving instant feedback, and deferring non-critical work.

questions.title: What is Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) and how is it calculated?
questions.quick: CLS measures unexpected movement of visible content during a page's life. Each layout shift gets a score equal to impact fraction times distance fraction: how much of the viewport was affected multiplied by how far it moved. The metric reports the worst burst of shifts, using session windows of up to five seconds. Shifts that happen right after a user input, such as expanding a menu, are excluded. Good is 0.1 or less at the 75th percentile.
questions.revision: CLS = worst burst of unexpected layout shifts, each scored impact fraction × distance fraction; shifts right after user input don't count; good ≤0.1.
questions.detailed:
**CLS** quantifies how much visible content moves without the user asking it to. A classic example: the page renders, you go to tap a button, an image above loads, everything slides down, and you tap the wrong thing.

## Scoring
Each layout shift has:

```text
layout shift score = impact fraction × distance fraction
```

- **Impact fraction**: share of the viewport area covered by elements that moved (before and after positions combined).
- **Distance fraction**: the greatest distance an element moved, divided by the viewport's largest dimension.

Shifts are grouped into **session windows**: bursts separated by at least one second of calm, capped at five seconds. CLS reports the **largest window's total**, so a long-lived page is not penalised for accumulating tiny shifts forever.

## What counts
- Counted: elements moving without user intent, such as images, ads, banners and late content pushing things around.
- Not counted: shifts within about 500 ms after a discrete user input (click, key press), and movement produced by CSS `transform` animations because they do not change layout.

## Example
A vehicle card shows title and a "Buy now" link; then a promotional banner is inserted above them, pushing both down by 120 px on a phone. That moves a big part of the viewport a notable distance, producing a high score such as 0.2 to 0.3.

## Thresholds
Good is 0.1 or less, poor is above 0.25, measured at the 75th percentile.

## Common mistakes
- Believing CLS is a time measurement; it is a unitless score.
- Testing only the initial load: shifts also happen later during scrolling or after API calls.
- Using `top`/`margin` animations instead of `transform`.

questions.title: What causes CLS and how do you fix it?
questions.quick: CLS comes from content that changes size or appears without reserved space: images and iframes without dimensions, injected banners and consent bars, ads and embeds, late-rendered components and skeletons that do not match final size, and web fonts that swap with different metrics. The fix is to reserve space with width and height attributes or CSS aspect-ratio, use min-height slots for dynamic content, insert new content below the viewport or in reserved areas, and match fallback font metrics.
questions.revision: CLS fixes = reserve space before content arrives: image dimensions or aspect-ratio, sized slots for ads and banners, matching font metrics, no insertion above existing content.
questions.detailed: Layout shifts happen when the browser had to guess how much room content needs and guessed wrong. Reserve the space up front. | Cause | Fix | |---|---| | Images/video/iframes without dimensions | `width` and `height` attributes (browser derives aspect ratio) or CSS `aspect-ratio` | | Ads, embeds, promo banners injected late | Fixed-size or `min-height` slot, placeholder of the expected size | | Cookie/consent bar pushing page down | Overlay it (fixed position) or reserve its height from the start | | Client-rendered components, skeletons of wrong size | Skeleton that matches final dimensions; server render the shell | | Web fonts swapping | `font-display`, preload critical fonts, metric-matched fallback via `size-adjust`/`ascent-override` | | Content inserted above existing content | Insert below the fold, or only after user action | | Animations using layout properties | Animate `transform` and `opacity` instead | ```html ``` Note: with responsive CSS such as `img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }`, the width and height attributes still give the browser the intrinsic ratio so space is reserved before the file loads. ## Diagnosing Use the Layout Shift regions in DevTools Performance, Lighthouse's "avoid large layout shifts" audit, or the `layout-shift` entries in RUM (including their `sources` nodes) to find the exact elements. ## Common mistakes - Fixing images but leaving a late banner or font swap. - Hiding content with `display:none` then showing it above other content. - Assuming lazy loading is harmless: a lazy image without dimensions still shifts when it loads.

questions.title: Compare LCP, INP and CLS: what does each measure and what typically breaks it?
questions.quick: LCP asks how fast the main content appears, INP asks how fast the page responds to interactions, and CLS asks whether content stays still. LCP is mostly a network and resource-discovery problem: server response, images, render-blocking assets. INP is a main-thread CPU problem: long tasks, heavy handlers, over-rendering. CLS is a layout problem: missing dimensions, late injected content, font swaps. Good targets are 2.5 seconds, 200 milliseconds and 0.1.
questions.revision: LCP=load (network, discovery), INP=interaction (main-thread CPU), CLS=stability (reserved space). Targets 2.5s, 200ms, 0.1 at p75.
questions.detailed:
The three metrics cover different phases of experience and usually fail for different reasons, so the fixes rarely overlap.

| | LCP | INP | CLS |
|---|---|---|---|
| Question | Is the main content here yet? | Does the page react to me? | Does it stay put? |
| Phase | Load | Whole visit, interactions | Whole visit, layout |
| Unit | Seconds | Milliseconds | Unitless score |
| Good (p75) | ≤ 2.5 s | ≤ 200 ms | ≤ 0.1 |
| Poor | > 4 s | > 500 ms | > 0.25 |
| Dominant bottleneck | Network, TTFB, resource discovery | Main-thread JavaScript | Unreserved space, font swaps |
| First tools to reach for | CDN, image priority, caching | Profiling long tasks, splitting work | Dimensions, aspect-ratio, slots |

## Interactions between them
- Heavy JavaScript can hurt all three: it delays LCP (render delay), blocks INP (long tasks), and can cause CLS when components render late.
- Lazy loading helps INP and bandwidth but can harm LCP if applied to the hero, and harm CLS if it lacks reserved space.
- Server rendering often improves LCP but can worsen INP through hydration cost.
- A web font strategy touches LCP (text rendering delay) and CLS (swap shifts).

## Why this matters in diagnosis
Which metric is failing tells you which team and tool to involve: infra and CDN for LCP, front-end runtime for INP, design system and content for CLS.

## Common mistakes
- Applying one generic "make it faster" fix to all three.
- Optimising LCP and unknowingly regressing INP by shipping a larger hydrated bundle.

questions.title: What is TTFB and how does it affect LCP?
questions.quick: TTFB, Time to First Byte, is the time from starting a navigation until the first byte of the HTML response arrives. It includes redirects, DNS, connection and TLS setup, and server or edge processing. It is not a Core Web Vital, but it is a floor under LCP: nothing renders before it. If TTFB is 2 seconds and the image needs another second, LCP is about 3 seconds. A guideline target is roughly 800 milliseconds or less.
questions.revision: TTFB = navigation start to first response byte (redirects, DNS, TLS, server time). Not a CWV, but it sets a floor for LCP; aim ~0.8s or less.
questions.detailed:
**TTFB** covers everything before the first byte of the document arrives:

{{diagram:ttfb-path}}

- Redirects (for example HTTP to HTTPS, or locale redirects)
- DNS lookup and TCP/TLS connection setup
- Request travel time to the edge or origin
- Server or edge processing (SSR rendering, API calls, database queries)

It is **not** a Core Web Vital, but because the browser cannot parse HTML, discover the hero image or start rendering before the first byte, every millisecond of TTFB is added to LCP.

## Worked example (illustrative numbers)
| TTFB | Remaining time to load and render LCP element | LCP |
|---|---|---|
| 2.0 s | 1.0 s | about 3.0 s (fails the 2.5 s target) |
| 0.4 s | 1.0 s | about 1.4 s |

Even a perfectly optimised image cannot rescue a page whose first byte arrives at 2 s.

## How to improve it
- Cache HTML at the CDN where content allows; use `stale-while-revalidate` for freshness.
- Remove redirect hops and use HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 with preconnect for needed origins.
- Make the origin faster: reduce SSR work, cache API and database results, avoid cold starts.
- Use streaming SSR so useful HTML flushes early.
- Keep users close to compute (edge delivery, regional origins).

## Common mistakes
- Quoting TTFB of a cached edge hit and ignoring cache-miss responses, which real users also experience.
- Optimising front-end assets while the backend dominates.
- Ignoring personalisation that forces every request to bypass cache.
